docs.t: Judge Allison D. Burroughs (D. Mass.) — Trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Allison D. Burroughs, D. Mass.. Trial (trap): Trial runs 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. with a lunch break and an afternoon break. Pre-mark all exhibits, agreed or not, and have a hard copy of exhibits for the judge at trial (no advance courtesy copies). The judge questions jurors for cause; jurors are not seated in the box, and the parties alternate peremptory strikes on anyone, in any order, with very limited attorney follow-up. Civil juries are 12; criminal alternates at least 2, up to 4. No speaking objections: objections are limited to 3 words. Chalks are disfavored in openings (allowed if unopposed) and more acceptable in closings. The podium is not required.

docs.t: Judge Allison D. Burroughs (D. Mass.) — Criminal and sentencing
docs.x: Judge Allison D. Burroughs, D. Mass.. Criminal and sentencing: The judge typically handles criminal discovery, generally refers release or modification motions to the magistrate judge, and holds detention-review hearings if requested, helpful, and the outcome is in question. Sentencing memoranda are not required but always helpful. Expedited sentencing may be considered where the potential sentence is shorter than 12 weeks and neither party objects.

docs.t: Judge Allison D. Burroughs (D. Mass.) — Junior lawyers and contact
docs.x: Judge Allison D. Burroughs, D. Mass.. Junior lawyers and contact: The judge encourages getting associates and junior attorneys to participate as often as possible. Courtroom 17, 5th floor, Moakley Courthouse, Boston. Courtroom deputy Karen Folan, 617-748-4232.

docs.t: Judge Denise J. Casper (D. Mass.) — Summary judgment Word-document SUF procedure (trap)
docs.x: Judge Denise J. Casper, D. Mass.. Summary judgment Word-document SUF procedure (trap): The movant must serve the non-movant with a Word version of its statement of undisputed facts when filing the motion and supporting materials. The non-movant files its response on that same Word document, answering each fact paragraph by paragraph with page references to affidavits, depositions, or other record documents if disputed; any separate disputed material facts go in a separate section at the end, also paragraph by paragraph with record cites. The non-movant files it on ECF and serves it in Word with the opposition. The movant may respond to the separately identified facts on the same Word document, filed with its reply.

docs.t: Judge Denise J. Casper (D. Mass.) — Briefing and motion hearings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Denise J. Casper, D. Mass.. Briefing and motion hearings (trap): Reply briefs are typically allowed, but only with a motion for leave; surreplies typically are not. When a reply limit is set, it is usually 10 pages. The judge typically holds hearings on motions to dismiss and for summary judgment and often sets time limits on argument, depending on the case. Post-argument briefs are allowed rarely, only when something counsel could not have anticipated comes up at argument.

docs.t: Judge Denise J. Casper (D. Mass.) — Remote appearances
docs.x: Judge Denise J. Casper, D. Mass.. Remote appearances: Initial scheduling and status conferences (civil) and initial pretrial and status conferences (criminal) are routinely held by Zoom; if the judge shifts to in-person, a Zoom conference will still be considered on request, particularly for out-of-town counsel. A civil non-evidentiary motion hearing may be held by Zoom for good cause if the other side does not object. On Zoom, stay muted when not speaking, use both video and audio, and display your first and last name (not initials or a phone number); if you lack a camera, contact courtroom deputy Lisa Hourihan in advance. Speak slowly and clearly. By phone, use a land line if possible, do not use the speaker function or a voice-activated system, pause to avoid speaking over others, and identify yourself before speaking. Recording or broadcasting proceedings is prohibited (L.R. 83.3(a);

docs.t: Judge Denise J. Casper (D. Mass.) — Scheduling and status conferences
docs.x: Judge Denise J. Casper, D. Mass.. Scheduling and status conferences: At the scheduling conference the judge asks whether plaintiff has made a settlement demand and, if not (or if defendants have not responded), sets a short date to do so; the judge also asks about interest in mediation before a magistrate judge. The judge sets fact discovery, amendment, summary judgment, and (if expected) expert deadlines, and may set an early Daubert date. Be ready to discuss sequencing or bifurcation and whether expert discovery can wait until after summary judgment (for example, damages-only experts). Raise any ESI proposal in the joint statement and say at the conference if you plan to file a protective order. The scheduling-order template sets a status conference (typically after fact discovery) and an initial pretrial conference, with a joint pretrial memorandum under L.R. 16.5(d) due 5 business da

docs.t: Judge Denise J. Casper (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Denise J. Casper, D. Mass.. Discovery: Discovery motions are typically referred to the magistrate judge and decided on the papers without a hearing. If the conferral looks pro forma despite the certification, the judge may order further conferral before acting or referring the motion.

docs.t: Judge Denise J. Casper (D. Mass.) — Default judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Denise J. Casper, D. Mass.. Default judgment (trap): After a notice of default, the moving party must take necessary and appropriate action within 30 days of the standing order, comply with Rule 55 (particularly its affidavit requirements), and file a proposed form of default judgment (the judge’s posted form) with the motion. The defaulted party has 14 days to file a substantiated opposition and request a hearing. If the movant cannot act in time, it must file an affidavit on the case status showing good cause why the case should stay on the docket; otherwise its claims are dismissed for want of prosecution.

docs.t: Judge Denise J. Casper (D. Mass.) — Pretrial
docs.x: Judge Denise J. Casper, D. Mass.. Pretrial: Trial dates are set at the post-fact-discovery status conference if no summary judgment motion is coming, otherwise after the motion is decided; criminal trial dates at the initial pretrial conference (confer about a date beforehand). Motions in limine are typically due 2 weeks before trial; oppositions, witness and exhibit lists, proposed voir dire, and jury instructions about 1 week before. Provide Word versions of proposed jury instructions and the verdict form. Motions in limine are heard at the final pretrial conference; Daubert motions are usually resolved earlier. Trial briefs are not required but are helpful on issues to resolve before trial, witness-scheduling issues, or special procedures (for example, a jury questionnaire, which is used only in complex cases and should be proposed at the initial pretrial conference).

docs.t: Judge Denise J. Casper (D. Mass.) — Exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Denise J. Casper, D. Mass.. Exhibits (trap): Courtesy copies of trial exhibits are required in electronic form only, typically the week before trial. Pre-mark agreed exhibits with numbers and disputed exhibits with letters, and provide a joint chart giving the basis for each objection and the proponent’s response.

docs.t: Judge Denise J. Casper (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Denise J. Casper, D. Mass.. Trial: Trial days are often 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., but some trials run full days (9 a.m. to 4 p.m.) or a mix, discussed at the initial pretrial conference. In civil cases the judge typically sets a total time limit covering openings, all examinations, and closings, after conferring with counsel. The judge conducts voir dire of the whole panel, then sees jurors who answered yes at sidebar; peremptories alternate by round (plaintiff/government first in round one). The first 8 remaining jurors sit in civil cases and the first 14 in criminal cases (2 alternates); no attorney voir dire. Use the podium for witness examination (short redirect or recross may be from counsel table). Disclose chalks to opposing counsel before openings or closings. Rebuttal cases only rarely, for issues counsel could not reasonably have anticipated. The judge circulates a draft charge a

docs.t: Judge Denise J. Casper (D. Mass.) — Criminal and sentencing
docs.x: Judge Denise J. Casper, D. Mass.. Criminal and sentencing: Criminal discovery matters and bail-modification motions after referral back are typically sent to the magistrate judge; detention-review motions are usually heard. Suppression motions are set for hearing once ripe. Sentencing memoranda are not required, but it should be a rare case without one; they help when they explain the recommendation and analyze the PSR. Expedited sentencing is considered to avoid “dead time” under the typical 12 weeks to sentencing; postponement only for specified, compelling reasons and for a defined period. Victims speak from the podium and address the court. In revocation matters, tell the clerk ahead of time whether an evidentiary hearing is needed.

docs.t: Judge Denise J. Casper (D. Mass.) — Junior lawyers
docs.x: Judge Denise J. Casper, D. Mass.. Junior lawyers: The judge strongly encourages relatively inexperienced attorneys to appear at conferences, argue motions, and examine witnesses, held to the highest professional standards. Every attorney appearing must have authority commensurate with the proceeding (for example, to commit to a schedule and address mediation), and junior lawyers in complex evidentiary hearings should be supervised by a more experienced attorney unless the court grants leave.

docs.t: Judge John J. McConnell Jr. (D.R.I.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge John J. McConnell Jr., D.R.I.. Discovery disputes: No discovery motion may be filed until you’ve tried in good faith to resolve the dispute with opposing counsel. If that fails, you must first have an informal conference with the Court, arranged through the judge’s case manager. This language is now in the district judges’ pretrial scheduling orders (court notice of August 2, 2021). Chief Judge McConnell’s case manager (as listed in the 2021 notice): Ryan Jackson, (401) 752-7213.

docs.t: Judge John J. McConnell Jr. (D.R.I.) — Rule 16(b) scheduling conference
docs.x: Judge John J. McConnell Jr., D.R.I.. Rule 16(b) scheduling conference: Lead counsel must confer beforehand about exchanging information, disputed facts, legal issues, the discovery contemplated, settlement, and possible referral to ADR. Each party asserting a claim (including a counterclaim or cross-claim) files a written statement of no more than three pages summarizing the facts and legal issues, at least seven days before the conference in the standard notice. Trial counsel, including counsel admitted pro hac vice, must attend unless excused.

docs.t: Judge John J. McConnell Jr. (D.R.I.) — Final pretrial conference
docs.x: Judge John J. McConnell Jr., D.R.I.. Final pretrial conference: Be ready to give the trial length and scheduling conflicts, a witness list in order with the length of direct and cross, any special witness needs, how exhibits will be presented and which come in without objection, and whether testimony will be by deposition, with designation deadlines. Unless the court orders otherwise, motions in limine and memoranda are due 14 days before jury empanelment, with objections 7 days after that. Trial counsel must confer and give the court a paper list of exhibits to be admitted without objection 7 days before empanelment.

docs.t: Judge John J. McConnell Jr. (D.R.I.) — Trial notice and settlement
docs.x: Judge John J. McConnell Jr., D.R.I.. Trial notice and settlement: Voir dire questions and, in civil cases, a brief statement of the facts are due by the date in the trial notice. A settlement must be reported to the clerk and a stipulation of dismissal filed at least seven days before empanelment, or jury costs and fees may be assessed for unreasonable lateness.

docs.t: Judge John J. McConnell Jr. (D.R.I.) — ADR referral
docs.x: Judge John J. McConnell Jr., D.R.I.. ADR referral: A standard order refers cases to mediation. Parties, lead counsel, and a representative with full settlement authority must attend in person. Mediation briefs go to the mediator only, not to the other side. No extension of the mediation date without the mediator’s written assent, and the parties must participate in good faith.

docs.t: Judge Gina R. Méndez-Miró (D.P.R.) — Contacting chambers
docs.x: Judge Gina R. Méndez-Miró, D.P.R.. Contacting chambers: Don’t call chambers at any time, especially the law clerks’ lines, about case-related questions, scheduling, CM/ECF technical help, calendaring, or court appearances. A motion is the only appropriate way to contact the Court. Chambers staff may not give time estimates for rulings, legal advice, or discuss the merits of any pending case. Every filing on CM/ECF is reviewed daily, so urgent matters in a filing will get prompt attention.

docs.t: Judge Gina R. Méndez-Miró (D.P.R.) — Who to contact instead
docs.x: Judge Gina R. Méndez-Miró, D.P.R.. Who to contact instead: Criminal matters go to the Courtroom Deputy. Questions about filings go to the assigned Docket Clerk or Docket Quality Analyst. CM/ECF technical questions go to the Help Desk at (787) 772-3449. Law clerks don’t handle the calendar or CM/ECF.

docs.t: Judge Gina R. Méndez-Miró (D.P.R.) — Consequences and expectations
docs.x: Judge Gina R. Méndez-Miró, D.P.R.. Consequences and expectations: Any direct or indirect violation will result in sanctions. Attorneys are absolutely prohibited from contacting chambers about their appearance before the Court, and are expected to appear on time. Calls to the Court and Clerk’s Office must conform to the Canons of Professional Conduct and Judicial Ethics.

docs.t: Judge Raúl M. Arias-Marxuach (D.P.R.) — Contacting chambers
docs.x: Judge Raúl M. Arias-Marxuach, D.P.R.. Contacting chambers: Chief Judge Arias-Marxuach issued a Standing Order on September 20, 2019 on communications by counsel and their staff with chambers. I couldn’t read it, but Judge Méndez-Miró’s 2023 order says it was adapted from Judge Arias-Marxuach’s order on the same subject: no calls to chambers or law clerks about case matters, scheduling, or filing help, and a motion is the proper way to contact the Court. Read the order itself before relying on this.

docs.t: Judge Raúl M. Arias-Marxuach (D.P.R.) — Other standing orders
docs.x: Judge Raúl M. Arias-Marxuach, D.P.R.. Other standing orders: Judge Arias-Marxuach has issued amended standing orders of disqualification (the latest listed is dated January 2, 2024) and a general standing order on transcript requests in criminal cases. I found no civil motion-practice order for the judge.

docs.t: Judge Brian E. Murphy (D. Mass.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian E. Murphy, D. Mass.. Summary judgment (trap): When it files, the movant must serve a Word version of its statement of undisputed facts and all supporting materials on the non-movant. The non-movant responds in that same Word document, paragraph by paragraph, with page references to the record for any dispute, adds any additional facts at the end continuing the numbering, files it on ECF, and serves the Word file back. The movant then responds to the additional facts in the same document, filed with its reply, so the court has a single document containing all facts and objections. Admissibility disputes go in the statement of facts or the opposition (Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(2)), not in separate motions to strike. Cross-movants exchange a single statement of facts covering both motions. Oppositions are due within 21 days after service of the motion.

docs.t: Judge Brian E. Murphy (D. Mass.) — Reply briefs (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian E. Murphy, D. Mass.. Reply briefs (trap): A reply needs no leave if it is no more than 5 pages, double-spaced, and filed within 7 days (excluding weekends and legal holidays) after service of the opposition. Any other reply or sur-reply needs leave, and the proposed brief may be filed with the motion for leave; the survey says such additional briefs are typically capped at 5 pages.

docs.t: Judge Brian E. Murphy (D. Mass.) — Motions and hearings
docs.x: Judge Brian E. Murphy, D. Mass.. Motions and hearings: Hearings on motions to dismiss are decided case by case; parties may request one, but the court may rule on the papers. Summary judgment motions are generally heard. No general time limits. Post-argument briefs may be requested by the court or proposed by a party and are allowed if helpful. Courtesy copies are appreciated, especially for large records, but not required beyond the Local Rules. Civil status conferences are typically remote, and civil motion hearings can be remote if counsel is not local and asks.

docs.t: Judge Brian E. Murphy (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Brian E. Murphy, D. Mass.. Discovery: The judge prefers to resolve discovery motions, usually holds a hearing, and typically rules from the bench after reviewing the filings. Comply carefully with L.R. 37.1(b). Emergency discovery motions are considered only if the parties have meaningfully conferred and tried to resolve the issue themselves. Bifurcation is generally not allowed, and a protective order should be sought as soon as the need arises. Motions to compel, for protective orders, to quash, or to strike discovery responses must be filed by the close of the relevant fact or expert discovery period, absent good cause.

docs.t: Judge Brian E. Murphy (D. Mass.) — Scheduling and case management
docs.x: Judge Brian E. Murphy, D. Mass.. Scheduling and case management: The scheduling order runs through summary judgment and staggers expert discovery (plaintiff’s experts disclosed and deposed before defendant’s). The court asks about interest in mediation at the scheduling conference. A status conference is held near the close of discovery and on request; a status report on discovery, expected expert discovery and dispositive motions, and interest in mediation is due 2 days before. Extension requests must be by motion stating the original dates, the number of prior requests and their outcome, the reasons, and the other side’s position, plus remaining discovery and a specific completion date; absent an emergency, file at least 48 hours before the deadline. Good cause is required.

docs.t: Judge Brian E. Murphy (D. Mass.) — Pretrial
docs.x: Judge Brian E. Murphy, D. Mass.. Pretrial: The civil trial date is set after any dispositive motions are decided. The parties must file an L.R. 16.5(d) pretrial memorandum 5 business days before the initial pretrial conference (omitting the items in L.R. 16.5(d)(2) and (3)); lead trial counsel must attend. Deadlines for voir dire, instructions, verdict forms, witness and exhibit lists, and motions in limine are set at the initial pretrial conference, typically three weeks before trial. Send the courtroom clerk a Word courtesy copy of proposed voir dire, verdict forms, and jury instructions. A trial brief is required. The court aims to resolve all motions in limine and Daubert motions before empanelment.

docs.t: Judge Brian E. Murphy (D. Mass.) — Trial exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian E. Murphy, D. Mass.. Trial exhibits (trap): Number every exhibit with a unique number, with no letters and no separate plaintiff’s or defendant’s exhibits. Groups may use decimals (for example, 13.1, 13.2); numbers never change even if an exhibit is excluded or not offered, and gaps are fine. Provide a courtesy copy of trial exhibits in a tabbed binder one week before trial.

docs.t: Judge Brian E. Murphy (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Brian E. Murphy, D. Mass.. Trial: Trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., and the court may set time limits. The judge seats 12 jurors in civil trials and 2 alternates in criminal trials. Voir dire is discussed at the final pretrial conference; counsel may generally ask follow-up questions during individual voir dire. If a questionnaire is wanted, file a joint questionnaire noting disagreements before the final pretrial conference. Podium use is not required; tell opposing counsel before using chalks. The court circulates a draft charge before trial for redline changes and resolves disagreements at a charge conference shortly before closings; rebuttal, if allowed, is strictly limited.

docs.t: Judge Brian E. Murphy (D. Mass.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Brian E. Murphy, D. Mass.. Criminal cases: The trial date is set at the initial status hearing after the case returns from the magistrate judge. The judge does not handle criminal discovery and usually holds hearings on detention reviews. Sentencing memoranda are not required in every case but are helpful whenever recommendations differ. Expedited sentencing is considered whenever the parties seek it, and postponement for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Richard G. Stearns (D. Mass.) — Courtesy copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard G. Stearns, D. Mass.. Courtesy copies (trap): The May 19, 2008 standing order requires paper courtesy copies of Markman filings, discovery-dispute papers, and dispositive motions, oppositions, replies, or sur-replies (with affidavits and exhibits) over 20 pages, stamped “Courtesy Copy for the Court: DO NOT SCAN.” “Dispositive” includes motions to dismiss, for summary judgment, to suppress, for preliminary relief, for judgment as a matter of law, and in limine; “discovery motion” includes motions to compel and for protective orders. The judge’s survey answer differs: for dispositive motions, courtesy copies are expected if the papers exceed 25 pages, delivered to the Clerk’s Office marked for Stearns Chambers. The survey is undated, so it is unclear which threshold is current.

docs.t: Judge Richard G. Stearns (D. Mass.) — Motions and briefing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard G. Stearns, D. Mass.. Motions and briefing (trap): Absent pre-approval in exceptional circumstances, each party gets one summary judgment motion of no more than 30 pages. Replies only with leave, and then 10 pages or less. Patent cases (June 3, 2021 order): summary judgment 30 pages total per party for moving briefs, 30 for oppositions, and 10 for replies; Daubert 20, 20, and 5; each motion in limine 5 pages, and the court may or may not call for a response or may reserve the issue for trial. Hearings on motions to dismiss and for summary judgment are held only if the papers suggest one would help; a summary judgment hearing may be by Zoom on request. Post-argument briefs only if the law is in flux or the case turns on circumstances not reasonably ascertainable at the hearing.

docs.t: Judge Richard G. Stearns (D. Mass.) — Hearings and remote appearances
docs.x: Judge Richard G. Stearns, D. Mass.. Hearings and remote appearances: Criminal hearings are held in Courtroom 21; Rule 11 proceedings and sentencings may be by video if the defendant, advised by counsel, waives personal presence. Civil hearings: the parties may jointly elect in-person or video. If they disagree, each files a position statement of no more than 1 page. The election or position statements must be filed on the docket at least 5 days before the hearing. In civil trials, until further notice, witnesses may testify by Zoom or other live video by agreement, on a showing of undue expense, hardship, or health risk from travel, or if the court so orders.

docs.t: Judge Richard G. Stearns (D. Mass.) — Scheduling (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard G. Stearns, D. Mass.. Scheduling (trap): The judge generally does not convene in-person scheduling or status conferences and instead issues a scheduling order based on the parties’ suggestions; written status reports may be requested. The posted Notice of Scheduling Conference prefers senior counsel (or substitute counsel with binding authority); out-of-state or Western Division counsel may call the deputy clerk at 617-748-9162 to ask to participate by phone. The notice requires the L.R. 16.1 joint statement 7 days before the conference and plaintiff’s written settlement proposal 14 days before; a discovery plan over 270 days needs a statement of exceptional circumstances. The court does not extend the pretrial schedule beyond the trial or dispositive-motion dates, and noncompliance may draw sanctions. docs.t: Judge Richard G. Stearns (D. Mass.) — Related actions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard G. Stearns, D. Mass.. Related actions (trap): File a Notice of Related Actions with the L.R. 16.1(d) joint statement, listing every known related action before any court or agency (forum, filing date, parties, brief description, and status), and a Supplemental Notice within 14 days after any related action begins or ends. The duty is continuing and applies to pro se litigants; leave to file under seal may be sought.

docs.t: Judge Richard G. Stearns (D. Mass.) — Discovery and protective orders
docs.x: Judge Richard G. Stearns, D. Mass.. Discovery and protective orders: The judge typically resolves discovery motions on the papers, without a hearing. For urgency, request a shortened response period in the filing. In complex cases (for example, patent, trade secret, or securities fraud), until a stipulated protective order is entered, a default protective order applies: material designated “Confidential Pursuant to the Court’s Default PO” may be seen only by outside counsel and the court and their personnel. Execute a tailored protective order early. Experts may testify only within the scope of their reports. Treating physicians may produce their records early in fact discovery instead of a Rule 26 report. The judge does not set Daubert deadlines; bifurcated discovery only in sizeable class or MDL cases. Patent cases generally follow L.R. 16.6, with Markman briefs ranking disputed terms

docs.t: Judge Richard G. Stearns (D. Mass.) — Civil jury trial filings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard G. Stearns, D. Mass.. Civil jury trial filings (trap): By the date in the trial order, file stipulated facts, a witness list (name and town or business address), a joint list of unobjected-to exhibits numbered in one sequence (deemed admitted), a list of objected-to exhibits lettered in one sequence, motions in limine with authority, a trial memorandum on foreseeable legal disputes, a trial-length estimate, substantive jury instructions with authority, verdict questions, voir dire questions, and a neutral statement of the case for the venire. Deposition and interrogatory designations: mark offered testimony by page and line in yellow highlighter with cover pages, exchange hard copies, mark objections in pink with the basis in the margin, and submit a hard copy to the courtroom clerk by the set date. Do not submit boilerplate instructions; the judge’s standard civil and crim

docs.t: Judge Richard G. Stearns (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Richard G. Stearns, D. Mass.. Trial: Civil jury trials run 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on impanelment day and 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. thereafter; each side is charged for its cross-examination time. Openings are typically limited to 25 minutes and closings to 45, and trials over a week have strictly enforced time limits. Trial briefs are required in civil and criminal cases. Motions in limine, voir dire, instructions, and witness and exhibit lists are due 2 weeks before trial (the defendant need not produce a witness list). Courtesy copies of trial exhibits, in the form to be offered, are due 1 week before trial. Motions in limine are usually decided in advance, except in bench trials. No sidebar conferences during trial. No attorney voir dire; 8 civil jurors and 2 criminal alternates. Podium use is optional. Chalks are encouraged if consistent with Rules 1006 and 611. Counsel get the proposed instr

docs.t: Judge Richard G. Stearns (D. Mass.) — Bench trials
docs.x: Judge Richard G. Stearns, D. Mass.. Bench trials: Jointly file stipulated facts, a numbered list of unobjected-to exhibits and a lettered list of objected-to exhibits, witness lists, deposition designations by page and line with objections (rulings must be sought before trial to preserve them), motions in limine, and a trial-length estimate based on 9:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. days. Evidentiary motions are taken up during trial rather than in limine. Each side files separately numbered proposed findings and conclusions after trial, on a briefing schedule set at its close (and after the transcript is produced).

docs.t: Judge Richard G. Stearns (D. Mass.) — Criminal trials and sentencing
docs.x: Judge Richard G. Stearns, D. Mass.. Criminal trials and sentencing: The criminal trial order requires stipulated facts, a government witness list naming the case agent at counsel table, defense alibi and other witnesses to mention at voir dire, government expert qualifications and Rule 16 summaries (and reciprocal defense disclosures), pre-marked numbered government and defendant exhibits, motions in limine, a trial memorandum, a length estimate (9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Monday, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Tuesday to Friday), instructions, voir dire, and any equipment requests. A final pretrial conference is set at 3 p.m. Bail-modification motions after referral back go to the magistrate judge; detention reviews are usually heard. Sentencing memoranda help when extenuating or aggravating factors are at issue; expedited sentencing is considered for minor offenses, immigration matters, and custody near the l

docs.t: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni (D. Mass.) — Confidentiality agreements, not protective orders (trap)
docs.x: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni, D. Mass.. Confidentiality agreements, not protective orders (trap): The judge encourages parties to sign confidentiality agreements where they will facilitate discovery and discourages filing proposed protective orders absent special circumstances. Agreements covering discovery must be filed with the court. The court takes notice of these agreements but does not adopt or endorse them as court orders; in a dispute it considers the agreement with other factors when a party moves for relief. Parties may still seek a Rule 26(c) protective order or other order in extraordinary circumstances.

docs.t: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni (D. Mass.) — Default judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni, D. Mass.. Default judgment (trap): After a notice of default, move for default judgment within 30 days of the standing order (or, if not all parties in a multi-party case have defaulted, no later than 14 days after entry of judgment or when the court sets). Comply with Rule 55, include affidavits showing the amount of damages, and submit a form of default judgment like the Appendix A form. The defaulted party has 14 days to file a substantiated opposition and request a hearing; the court then takes up the motion on the papers. A movant that does not file must submit an affidavit on the case status showing good cause, or its claims will be dismissed for want of prosecution.

docs.t: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni (D. Mass.) — Case management and discovery
docs.x: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni, D. Mass.. Case management and discovery: In Springfield the initial scheduling conference is held before the magistrate judge, who handles discovery issues; discovery motions are typically referred to the magistrate judge, without a hearing. The judge asks whether the parties have meaningfully discussed settlement or mediation. The judge holds a status conference 3–4 months before the trial date covering motions in limine, evidentiary and witness issues, trial length, and realistic settlement prospects. Daubert motions are scheduled 3–4 months before trial at the final pretrial conference. For pro se litigants, technical and deadline standards are relaxed slightly, but only until the litigant is on fair notice of the usual standards.

docs.t: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni (D. Mass.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni, D. Mass.. Motions: No courtesy copies are required for dispositive motions. Replies and surreplies are allowed on request for good cause, with page limits depending on the issues. Hearings on motions to dismiss and for summary judgment are often held, depending on the issues, generally without time limits, though the court may direct counsel to move on. The court may request post-argument briefs on a specific topic with a page limit, and will consider requests to supplement on narrowly identified issues.

docs.t: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni (D. Mass.) — Pretrial
docs.x: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni, D. Mass.. Pretrial: Pretrial deadlines are set in a scheduling order issued about 7–10 weeks before trial; some items are due a few weeks before trial, with motions in limine due earlier. No page limit for motions in limine; they are heard at the final pretrial conference, and many are reserved for ruling at trial. Trial briefs are not required unless complexity or other factors show a need to avoid interruptions at trial. Courtesy copies of trial exhibits are not required; pre-mark exhibits, coordinating with the clerk. A request for a jury questionnaire must be made by motion no later than the motion-in-limine deadline.

docs.t: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni, D. Mass.. Trial: Full trial days are usual. Civil time limits, if any, are set in the pretrial order. All voir dire questions are posed to the panel, whose members take written notes; jurors are then interviewed individually outside the courtroom by the judge and attorneys. Civil juries are typically 9; criminal trials seat 3 alternates. Podium use is counsel’s choice unless hearing or seeing is a problem. Chalks: the judge prefers the parties reach agreement. A rebuttal case requires a legitimate issue and a good-faith showing and offer. Jury instructions are requested by the midpoint of trial, with an opportunity to supplement or modify; the jury gets a written charge, and special verdict proposals will be considered.

docs.t: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni (D. Mass.) — Criminal and sentencing
docs.x: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni, D. Mass.. Criminal and sentencing: The judge resolves bail-modification motions after referral back (depending on circumstances and closeness to trial) and usually holds hearings on detention reviews. Initial pretrial conferences generally follow L.R. 117.1(a). Sentencing memoranda are not required but help in complex or multi-defendant cases. Victim statements should be in writing with the presentence report, with notice if a victim may speak in court. Any reasonable request to postpone sentencing is considered.

docs.t: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni (D. Mass.) — Junior lawyers
docs.x: Judge Mark G. Mastroianni, D. Mass.. Junior lawyers: The judge strongly encourages relatively inexperienced attorneys to participate in all proceedings, held to the highest professional standards, with authority commensurate with the proceeding; those examining witnesses in complex evidentiary hearings should be supervised by a more experienced attorney unless the court gives leave.

docs.t: Judge Julia Kobick (D. Mass.) — Reply briefs (trap)
docs.x: Judge Julia Kobick, D. Mass.. Reply briefs (trap): A reply needs no leave if it is no more than 8 pages, double-spaced, and filed within 7 days (excluding weekends and legal holidays) after service of the opposition. Any other reply or sur-reply needs leave, and the proposed brief may be filed with the motion for leave. The survey adds that page limits for replies and sur-replies are often set case by case, and sur-replies are allowed if warranted.

docs.t: Judge Julia Kobick (D. Mass.) — Motions and hearings
docs.x: Judge Julia Kobick, D. Mass.. Motions and hearings: Confer meaningfully before filing a dispositive motion. Motions to dismiss and summary judgment motions are usually heard, with no set time limits. If a topic arises at the hearing that the briefs do not fully address, the judge often grants leave for short supplemental briefs; post-argument briefs without leave granted orally at the hearing are rarely allowed. Use slide decks at motion hearings sparingly, if at all. No courtesy copies by default, but the judge sometimes orders them by docket order.

docs.t: Judge Julia Kobick (D. Mass.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge Julia Kobick, D. Mass.. Summary judgment: The non-moving party should put its response directly under each fact in the movant’s concise statement, so that each fact and response appear in one document. Oppositions are due within 21 days after service of the motion.

docs.t: Judge Julia Kobick (D. Mass.) — Scheduling conference
docs.x: Judge Julia Kobick, D. Mass.. Scheduling conference: Held in Courtroom 3, remotely, or by telephone, as the notice states; the survey says initial scheduling and status conferences are typically by Zoom. Plaintiff’s counsel must notify parties who have not yet appeared. The L.R. 16.1(B)(1) agenda may be omitted unless counsel have extra matters, it is a patent case, or the court directs one. Each defendant must respond in writing to plaintiff’s settlement proposal at least 7 days before the conference. The joint statement must add a concise summary of each side’s position on liability and relief, and state whether all parties consent to a magistrate judge (file the consent form jointly if so). A non-cooperating party must be identified in a separate statement. Propose completing fact discovery, expert discovery, and pretrial motions within one calendar year in a case of ordinary complexi

docs.t: Judge Julia Kobick (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Julia Kobick, D. Mass.. Discovery: The judge usually resolves discovery motions (sometimes referring them to a magistrate judge), holds hearings only for complex disputes or questions, and entertains emergency discovery motions rarely and only in true emergencies. Motions to compel, for protective orders, to quash, or to strike discovery responses must be filed by the close of the relevant fact or expert discovery period, absent good cause. The template schedule staggers expert discovery: plaintiff’s experts are disclosed and deposed before defendant’s.

docs.t: Judge Julia Kobick (D. Mass.) — Extensions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Julia Kobick, D. Mass.. Extensions (trap): Extension requests must be by motion stating the original dates, the number of prior requests and their outcome, the reasons, and the other side’s position (with reasons for any refusal), plus a summary of remaining discovery and a specific completion date. Good cause is required. Absent an emergency, file at least 48 hours before the deadline or appearance.

docs.t: Judge Julia Kobick (D. Mass.) — Status and pretrial conferences
docs.x: Judge Julia Kobick, D. Mass.. Status and pretrial conferences: A status conference is usually held after the close of fact discovery; a status report on discovery, expected expert discovery and dispositive motions, and interest in mediation is due 2 days before. Any party may request a conference on reasonable notice. The initial pretrial conference sets the trial date. The scheduling-order template requires an L.R. 16.5(d) pretrial memorandum 5 business days before it (omitting the items in L.R. 16.5(d)(2) and (3)), although the survey says nothing need be filed beforehand; follow your case’s order. Lead trial counsel must attend any pretrial conference. A later pretrial order sets deadlines for voir dire, instructions, verdict forms, witness and exhibit lists, and motions in limine, typically one to two months before trial. Motions in limine are decided at or before the final pretrial

docs.t: Judge Julia Kobick (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Julia Kobick, D. Mass.. Trial: Trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., and the judge meets counsel at 8:30 a.m. each morning to resolve anticipated objections. A trial brief is required. Stipulated exhibits should be pre-marked, and courtesy copies of trial exhibits are required (no set timing or form). The judge asks general voir dire of the panel, then individually questions jurors who answered yes; attorney voir dire is rare. The judge seats 10 jurors in civil trials and 2 alternates in criminal trials, and gives the jury a written charge. Chalks are allowed within reason.

docs.t: Judge Julia Kobick (D. Mass.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Julia Kobick, D. Mass.. Criminal cases: The judge does not handle criminal discovery and typically refers release-condition motions back to the magistrate judge, but usually holds hearings on detention reviews. Sentencing memoranda are required in every case. Expedited sentencing is considered when a detained defendant risks overserving the guideline range.

docs.t: Judge John G. Koeltl (S.D.N.Y.) — Letters and contact (trap)
docs.x: Judge John G. Koeltl, S.D.N.Y.. Letters and contact (trap): Communicate by letter filed on ECF and copied to all counsel; letters and letter-motions, with exhibits, may not exceed 3 pages. Do not file or send letters between counsel. Courtesy copies of letters and letter-motions are no longer accepted. For docketing, scheduling, and calendar matters, call Court Clerk Don Fletcher at (212) 805-0107, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. ECF filings are generally reviewed the next business day; if something needs immediate attention, email chambers (koeltlnysdchambers@nysd.uscourts.gov) after filing.

docs.t: Judge John G. Koeltl (S.D.N.Y.) — Adjournments and extensions
docs.x: Judge John G. Koeltl, S.D.N.Y.. Adjournments and extensions: File as ECF letter-motions stating the original date, the number of prior requests, whether they were granted, and whether the adversary consents (and if not, why). Sensitive requests may go by fax or mail. If other dates are affected, attach a proposed Revised Scheduling Order using only business days. Adjournments of a court appearance must be requested at least 48 hours ahead, absent an emergency.

docs.t: Judge John G. Koeltl (S.D.N.Y.) — Pre-motion conferences (trap)
docs.x: Judge John G. Koeltl, S.D.N.Y.. Pre-motion conferences (trap): A pre-motion conference is required before a motion to dismiss, a motion to amend, or a summary judgment motion; discovery motions follow Local Civil Rule 37.2. Request it by letter-motion. Confer under Rule 26(f) and give the court a Rule 26(f) report before the initial conference.

docs.t: Judge John G. Koeltl (S.D.N.Y.) — Briefs and courtesy copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge John G. Koeltl, S.D.N.Y.. Briefs and courtesy copies (trap): Civil memoranda are limited to 7,000 words (opening and opposition) and 2,800 words (reply), with a signed word-count certificate, a table of contents, and a table of authorities (none of which count). Double-space text and footnotes. No limits for criminal memoranda. Summary judgment memoranda must include their own statement of facts; a Local Rule 56.1 statement or affidavits are no substitute and may not be incorporated by reference. File each motion paper promptly after service, but the movant sends one full set of courtesy copies (including opposition papers) only once the motion is fully briefed, by mail and by email. Side binding preferred, Velo binding discouraged; memoranda single-sided, long exhibits double-sided. Courtesy copies of pleadings, marked as such, go to chambers as soon as practicable after filing. docs.t: Judge John G. Koeltl (S.D.N.Y.) — Diversity jurisdiction (trap)
docs.x: Judge John G. Koeltl, S.D.N.Y.. Diversity jurisdiction (trap): When jurisdiction rests solely on diversity, the invoking party must detail each party’s citizenship at the earliest opportunity, including every member of each LLC, LP, or LLP and that member’s citizenship. Individuals are citizens of their domicile, not residence; corporations of their state of incorporation and principal place of business.

docs.t: Judge John G. Koeltl (S.D.N.Y.) — Discovery schedule and protocols
docs.x: Judge John G. Koeltl, S.D.N.Y.. Discovery schedule and protocols: The judge’s form scheduling order expects discovery to be completed within 60 days of the first scheduling conference unless all counsel then stipulate to more time (no more than 60 more days). Expert disclosures are due at least 30 days before the close of discovery. Employment cases alleging adverse action (other than class actions and cases involving only hiring, harassment, FLSA, ADA accommodation, FMLA, or ERISA claims) follow the Initial Discovery Protocols posted on the judge’s page, which replace Rule 26(a)(1) disclosures. FLSA cases not pleaded as collective actions follow the separate FLSA Initial Discovery Protocols. Under both protocols, each side produces the listed documents and information within 30 days after the defendant’s responsive pleading or motion, objections are limited (Rule 26(b)(2)(B), and for FL

docs.t: Judge John G. Koeltl (S.D.N.Y.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge John G. Koeltl, S.D.N.Y.. Sealing: Beyond Rule 5.2 redactions, sealing or redaction needs a public motion or letter-motion under Standing Order 19-mc-00583 and ECF Rules section 6, with the proposed sealed document filed under seal and related to it; for redactions, file the redacted version publicly and a highlighted unredacted version under seal. Requests must be narrowly tailored under Lugosch; consent or a confidentiality agreement alone is not enough. Meet and confer to narrow first, and if sealing is sought for another party or a third party, notify it that it must file a letter justifying sealing within 3 days.

docs.t: Judge John G. Koeltl (S.D.N.Y.) — Default judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge John G. Koeltl, S.D.N.Y.. Default judgment (trap): After obtaining the Clerk’s Certificate of Default (ECF Rules section 16.1), proceed by order to show cause, not notice of motion: file a proposed order to show cause, an attorney’s affidavit on why default judgment is appropriate, and a proposed default judgment with a statement of damages. The proposed order to show cause must include the judge’s required text setting the defendants’ response date, the plaintiff’s reply date, and service and proof-of-service dates, and stating that no personal appearances are required.

docs.t: Judge John G. Koeltl (S.D.N.Y.) — Pretrial (civil)
docs.x: Judge John G. Koeltl, S.D.N.Y.. Pretrial (civil): The joint pretrial order must follow the judge’s form and include jurisdiction statements, claims and defenses to be tried (and those not to be tried), jury or non-jury and trial days, magistrate-judge consent status (without saying who consented), stipulations, witnesses (live or by deposition), deposition designations with cross-designations and objections, and exhibit lists marked with one star (no authenticity objection) or two stars (no objection at all). With it, file requests to charge and voir dire (jury) or proposed findings and conclusions (non-jury), motions in limine, and any pretrial memorandum. If a dispositive motion is made, the pretrial order is due 3 weeks after the decision and the ready-trial date is 4 weeks after it. After the ready-for-trial date, notify the court and adversaries in writing of trial or vacation confl

docs.t: Judge John G. Koeltl (S.D.N.Y.) — Criminal sentencing
docs.x: Judge John G. Koeltl, S.D.N.Y.. Criminal sentencing: Defense counsel must schedule the presentence interview to occur within 14 days of the plea or verdict, and the AUSA must give Probation the case summary within 14 days. The posted timetable: interview done by day 28, initial PSR on day 55, objections by day 69, final PSR on day 83. Defense sentencing submissions are due 14 days before sentencing and the government’s 8 days before. File all submissions on ECF, redacted under Rule 49.1, with support letters grouped in one document marked SENTENCING MEMORANDUM, and email courtesy copies to chambers.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth M. Karas (S.D.N.Y.) — Contact and conferences (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kenneth M. Karas, S.D.N.Y.. Contact and conferences (trap): No phone calls or faxes to chambers. Communicate by letter on ECF (sealed or sensitive letters by mail); email KarasNYSDChambers@nysd.uscourts.gov only for questions the rules don’t answer or matters needing immediate attention, and scheduling goes to Courtroom Deputy Dawn Bordes at that address. Don’t contact chambers to confirm a filing; ECF questions go to the Clerk’s Office or ECF Hotline. Civil conferences and proceedings other than trials are held by telephone unless ordered otherwise: dial (605) 472-5160, access code 4653066#. Criminal proceedings are in person. Principal trial counsel must appear at all conferences. Bringing laptops, tablets, or similar devices to court requires submitting the S.D.N.Y. electronic-devices form by email at least 3 days before the appearance.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth M. Karas (S.D.N.Y.) — Adjournments and extensions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kenneth M. Karas, S.D.N.Y.. Adjournments and extensions (trap): Request at least 5 business days before the scheduled appearance, absent an emergency, by ECF letter-motion stating the original dates, the number of prior requests, whether they were granted, and whether the adversary consents (and if not, why). In a case referred to a magistrate judge, interim discovery extensions go to the magistrate judge, but any extension past the discovery completion date goes to Judge Karas. The form scheduling order says no such extension will be granted unless the parties consent to the magistrate judge for all purposes.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth M. Karas (S.D.N.Y.) — Pre-motion letters and motions to dismiss (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kenneth M. Karas, S.D.N.Y.. Pre-motion letters and motions to dismiss (trap): A pre-motion conference is required for almost every civil motion; exceptions include orders to show cause, motions by incarcerated pro se litigants, pro hac vice, reargument, class certification, and Rule 6(b) and FRAP 4(a)(4)(A) motions. Discovery motions follow Local Civil Rule 37.2. For a motion to dismiss in a fully counseled case, the movant sends the nonmovant a letter (filed on the docket) laying out each argument with case law; it stays the time to answer. Within 7 days the nonmovant must state whether it will amend (with a proposed deadline) or stand on the pleading. If it doesn’t amend and the complaint is later dismissed on those grounds, dismissal may be with prejudice. Other pre-motion letters are limited to 3 pages, with 3-page responses due within 7 days. For motions with a scheduling-orde

docs.t: Judge Kenneth M. Karas (S.D.N.Y.) — Briefs and motion papers
docs.x: Judge Kenneth M. Karas, S.D.N.Y.. Briefs and motion papers: Memoranda are limited to 8,750 words (opening and opposition) and 3,500 words (reply), with a word-count certification (pro se handwritten or typed: 25 and 10 pages). Use 12-point font, double spacing, and 1-inch margins; 10 pages or more needs a table of contents. Cite Westlaw where possible. No sur-replies without permission. Attach a copy of the complaint to the moving papers. File all exhibits on ECF as text-searchable PDFs (media on a drive or disc); any deposition transcript filed must be complete, not excerpted. No paper or courtesy copies unless the court asks. Notices of motion and proposed orders to show cause must not fill in a hearing date; use “on a date and at a time designated by the Court.”

docs.t: Judge Kenneth M. Karas (S.D.N.Y.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kenneth M. Karas, S.D.N.Y.. Summary judgment (trap): The movant must give other parties an electronic copy of its Local Civil Rule 56.1 statement. The opponent must reproduce each entry in full, including record citations, with its response directly beneath; failure may result in the entry being deemed admitted. A statement of additional material facts must be a separate docket filing, not combined with the response.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth M. Karas (S.D.N.Y.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Kenneth M. Karas, S.D.N.Y.. Case management: The initial Rule 16 conference is generally set within 4 months of filing; plaintiff’s counsel distributes the notice. Before it, file a proposed case management and scheduling order on the judge’s form. The form contemplates initial disclosures within 14 days of the Rule 26(f) conference, fact discovery of no more than 120 days absent unique complexity, depositions only after all parties respond to initial document requests, and non-party depositions after party depositions. Interim deadlines may be extended on consent if the completion date holds. Counsel must meet for at least one hour on settlement within 2 weeks after fact discovery closes.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth M. Karas (S.D.N.Y.) — Default judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kenneth M. Karas, S.D.N.Y.. Default judgment (trap): Proceed only by order to show cause, returnable in Courtroom 521, with the date and time left blank. Attach a proposed default judgment, a statement of damages, all pleadings, the affidavit of service of the summons and complaint, the Clerk’s certificate of no answer (if applicable), and an attorney’s affidavit covering service, whether judgment against fewer than all defendants is appropriate, each damages element with its basis, and why no inquest is needed. File on ECF for the Clerk’s review; after the judge signs, serve the conformed copy and file the affidavit of service on ECF before the return date.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth M. Karas (S.D.N.Y.) — FLSA settlements
docs.x: Judge Kenneth M. Karas, S.D.N.Y.. FLSA settlements: Any settlement of a case with an FLSA claim, including dismissal of the FLSA claim on consent, needs court approval under Cheeks. File the agreement and supporting papers on ECF unless sealing is permitted, and pay particular attention to the breadth of the release, confidentiality and non-disparagement terms, and attorney’s fees.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth M. Karas (S.D.N.Y.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Kenneth M. Karas, S.D.N.Y.. Sealing: Follow the ECF sealed-filing instructions; noncompliant documents won’t be filed. The motion is filed publicly and explains the reasons; electronically, file the proposed sealed document under seal and related to the motion (for redactions, also file the redacted version publicly and a highlighted unredacted version under seal). Under the traditional method, submit the proposed sealed document, the motion, and supporting papers on paper by hand or mail and also email them to chambers with redactions highlighted; if granted, file the unredacted document on paper under the sealed-records procedures.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth M. Karas (S.D.N.Y.) — Pretrial (civil)
docs.x: Judge Kenneth M. Karas, S.D.N.Y.. Pretrial (civil): The Joint Pretrial Order includes the Rule 26(a)(3) information plus jurisdiction statements, claims and defenses to be tried and not tried, jury or non-jury and trial days, magistrate-judge consent status, stipulations, witnesses, deposition designations, exhibit lists starred (one star: no authenticity objection; two: no objection), and whether the parties consent to a less-than-unanimous verdict. File with it: voir dire, verdict form, and requests to charge (jury; counsel must meet and confer to try for agreed submissions) or detailed proposed findings and conclusions (non-jury), motions in limine, and any pretrial memorandum. Objections and oppositions are due within 1 week of the pretrial order and no later than 2 days before trial.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth M. Karas (S.D.N.Y.) — Criminal cases and sentencing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kenneth M. Karas, S.D.N.Y.. Criminal cases and sentencing (trap): On assignment, the parties arrange a prompt conference with the defendant present to set discovery and motion schedules; the AUSA sends chambers the indictment and any complaint and, later, any plea agreement. The judge takes guilty pleas personally. Defense sentencing submissions must be served 2 weeks before sentencing (notify the court in writing promptly if the PSR is late) and the government’s 1 week before. File everything on ECF, letters grouped in one document marked SENTENCING MEMORANDUM; no courtesy copies. The five sensitive categories and six caution categories may be redacted without application; bring the redacted pages, marked, to sentencing for sealed filing. Any other redaction needs an application served and filed with the submission.

docs.t: Judge J. Paul Oetken (S.D.N.Y.) — Communications with chambers (trap)
docs.x: Judge J. Paul Oetken, S.D.N.Y.. Communications with chambers (trap): Communicate by letter or letter-motion on ECF; letters (including discovery letters) are limited to 4 pages, and letters seeking relief must be filed as letter-motions. No substantive emails without leave, and no courtesy copies unless ordered. For urgent matters needing attention in less than one business day, call chambers at (212) 805-0266, trying to include all counsel on the call. ECF filings are otherwise reviewed the next business day. Staff won’t answer substantive questions on ex parte calls. Hand deliveries go to the Court Security Officers at the 200 Worth Street entrance, not chambers; multimedia filings go there on a USB drive. Related-case filings must carry both docket numbers; after consolidation, file only in the lead docket.

docs.t: Judge J. Paul Oetken (S.D.N.Y.) — Filing format (trap)
docs.x: Judge J. Paul Oetken, S.D.N.Y.. Filing format (trap): Every submission should be a text-searchable PDF converted electronically, not scanned. Any amended or corrected filing must be filed with a redline showing all changes. Memoranda follow Local Civil Rule 7.1: 8,750 words (opening and opposition) and 3,500 words (reply). Memoranda of 3,500 words or more need a table of contents and a table of authorities; appendices must be indexed. No sur-replies without permission, and no copies of unpublished cases available on Westlaw or Lexis.

docs.t: Judge J. Paul Oetken (S.D.N.Y.) — Adjournments and extensions (trap)
docs.x: Judge J. Paul Oetken, S.D.N.Y.. Adjournments and extensions (trap): Seek the adversary’s consent first (the judge strongly encourages consenting to reasonable requests), then file a letter-motion, not a stipulation or proposed order, stating the old and new deadlines, the adversary’s position, prior requests and outcomes, and the reasons. Propose changes to any other affected deadlines. File at least 48 hours before the deadline or appearance; requests made after the deadline has passed will ordinarily be denied. Under the scheduling order, a request to extend fact discovery must be made at least 2 business days before the deadline, and parties may not halt discovery in anticipation of an extension.

docs.t: Judge J. Paul Oetken (S.D.N.Y.) — Conferences
docs.x: Judge J. Paul Oetken, S.D.N.Y.. Conferences: In-person conferences are in Courtroom 706, 40 Foley Square; to proceed remotely, confer with all counsel and file a letter-motion. Teleconferences use (855) 244-8681, attendee ID 2312 828 7066#; use a landline and headset, mute when not speaking, and identify yourself each time you speak. Principal trial counsel must attend all conferences absent leave. The judge encourages junior attorneys to argue and examine witnesses and may grant otherwise disfavored oral argument for that reason, but at least one attorney present must have authority to bind the client.

docs.t: Judge J. Paul Oetken (S.D.N.Y.) — Discovery and case management
docs.x: Judge J. Paul Oetken, S.D.N.Y.. Discovery and case management: No pre-motion conferences except for discovery disputes. After an in-person or phone meet-and-confer, file a letter-motion of up to 4 pages representing that conferral failed; opposition (up to 4 pages) is due within 3 business days. The court may rule on the letters alone. Raising issues late in discovery is unlikely to succeed. File the proposed case management plan at least 7 calendar days before the initial conference. The form sets fact discovery at no more than 120 days after the initial conference, document requests and Local Civil Rule 33.3(a) interrogatories within 30 days of the conference, contention interrogatories at least 30 days before the close of discovery (no others without permission), and expert discovery within 45 days after fact discovery. The burden-of-proof party’s expert reports come first.

Include an attorney declaration covering the basis for default (with method and date of service), procedural history, whether damages can be set before the case is resolved against other defendants, each element of damages (interest, fees, costs), and whether an inquest is needed; plus a proposed judgment, the affidavit of service, and, if based on failure to answer, a Clerk’s certificate. Serve the motion on the defaulting party.

Discovery disputes (trap): After a good-faith meet and confer (in person, virtually, or by phone), file a single jointly composed letter-motion of no more than 1,750 words; separate and successive letters will not be read. docs.x: Judge Jesse M. Furman, S.D.N.Y.. Summary judgment and Daubert (trap): Absent good cause, no summary judgment in non-jury cases. Under the plan form, summary judgment and Daubert motions are due within 30 days after the later of fact or expert discovery; oppositions 2 weeks after service, replies 1 week. Cross-motions are briefed in four consolidated briefs (motion, combined cross-motion and opposition, combined reply and opposition, reply); propose the structure, schedule, and page limits in advance. Briefs need their own background and facts sections, not incorporation of the 56.1 statement. Include deposition indexes and text-searchable transcripts. Daubert motions are due by the dispositive-motion deadline, are not motions in limine, and require a single motion and memorandum even against multiple experts.

docs.x: Judge Jesse M. Furman, S.D.N.Y.. Default judgment, TROs, and settlements: Obtain a Clerk’s certificate of default well before any court deadline, then move under Rule 55(b)(2) and Local Civil Rule 55.2, not by order to show cause. Include an attorney declaration, a sworn damages statement, a memorandum covering service, its legality, subject-matter and personal jurisdiction, partial default, and why no inquest is needed, native calculation files (e.g., .xlsx) emailed to chambers, the proposed judgment, pleadings, affidavit of service, and a certificate of service. TROs: confer first unless Rule 65(b)(1) is met. Without notice, file under seal and email chambers with “URGENT: TRO” in the subject; on notice, file, serve, and email chambers copying all parties. The court will not retain jurisdiction to enforce a confidential settlement unless its terms are on the public record.

Expedited and emergency motions: A discrete, potentially dispositive legal issue may be resolved, by agreement or court order, on letter-briefs of up to 5 pages per party; the court aims to rule within 14 days of full submission or hearing. Orders to show cause and injunction motions require notice to opposing counsel (except in the most extraordinary circumstances) and an agreed proposed briefing schedule. For TROs and other emergency relief, also email all papers as text-searchable PDFs with “URGENT” in the subject line, a phone number, and the parties’ hearing availability over the next few days.

docs.t: Judge Victor Marrero (S.D.N.Y.) — Communications and courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge Victor Marrero, S.D.N.Y.. Communications and courtesy copies: Communicate by letter, filed on ECF or emailed to ChambersNYSDMarrero@nysd.uscourts.gov, with copies to all parties. Faxes (212-805-6382) are discouraged and limited to 5 pages; do not follow with hard copy. Phone calls only in urgent situations, with all parties on the line; for urgent matters email with “URGENT” in the subject line. One marked courtesy hard copy of all motion papers and pleadings goes to chambers when served or filed. Hand delivery requires advance permission by email or phone.

docs.t: Judge Victor Marrero (S.D.N.Y.) — Extensions and adjournments
docs.x: Judge Victor Marrero, S.D.N.Y.. Extensions and adjournments: Requests must be in writing and received at least 2 business days before the deadline or appearance, stating the number and disposition of prior requests and whether the adversary consents (and if not, why). If other case-plan dates are affected, attach a proposed revised Case Management Plan. The requesting party must notify all others of the ruling. Bankruptcy appeal briefing dates (Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8009) may be extended by stipulation submitted at least 2 business days before the brief is due.

docs.t: Judge Victor Marrero (S.D.N.Y.) — Discovery and case management
docs.x: Judge Victor Marrero, S.D.N.Y.. Discovery and case management: Unresolved discovery disputes go to the court in a joint letter after conferring, stating each side’s position and authority; the court may rule or refer chronic disputes to the magistrate judge. A joint status letter covering 8 listed items (including threshold issues, settlement prospects, magistrate-judge consent, and interest in the expedited trial option) and a proposed Case Management Plan on the judge’s form must be received at least 5 business days before the initial conference. Seek leave in the plan for more than 5 depositions per party, any deposition over 3 hours, or interrogatories or requests to admit over 7 single-spaced pages. The plan form sets fact discovery at 120 days (longer only with approval for complex cases), requires an hour-long settlement meeting after discovery, and bars summary judgment motions s

docs.t: Judge Victor Marrero (S.D.N.Y.) — Sealing and default judgments
docs.x: Judge Victor Marrero, S.D.N.Y.. Sealing and default judgments: Sealing or redaction motions follow standing order 19-mc-00583 and ECF Rules section 6, and must identify all parties who should have access to the sealed versions. Default judgment applications need notice to the defaulting party (first-class mail or courier if domestic, courier if international, or a Rule 4 method) and an affidavit on the claim, subject matter and personal jurisdiction, non-infancy/competence, and notice; a clerk’s certificate of default; a fee affidavit; the complaint; and a proposed judgment. Damages requests must not exceed the complaint’s principal amount, include supporting calculations and documentation, and cap interest at the applicable statutory rate; otherwise damages go to inquest.

docs.t: Judge Victor Marrero (S.D.N.Y.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Victor Marrero, S.D.N.Y.. Criminal cases: The AUSA must contact chambers promptly after assignment, send a courtesy copy of the charging documents, email to arrange an initial conference to set discovery and motion schedules (and confirm by letter), and arrange Speedy Trial exclusions. Arraignments, bail, and pleas go to the magistrate court in the first instance. Plea agreements or Pimentel letters are due in chambers at least 2 business days before the plea conference. Sentencing adjournment requests are due at least 2 business days ahead, after clearing a date with the law clerk; all sentencing submissions must be received at least 5 business days before sentencing.

docs.t: Judge Victor Marrero (S.D.N.Y.) — Pretrial submissions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Victor Marrero, S.D.N.Y.. Pretrial submissions (trap): At least 30 days before a firm trial date, civil parties submit a joint pretrial order (with the listed contents, including starred exhibits that draw objections) in hard copy and Word. Jury cases add a 10-page pretrial memorandum, joint voir dire, joint requests to charge with authority, and a joint list of names likely to be mentioned; bench trials add a 15-page memorandum and proposed findings and conclusions. Motions in limine: oppositions due 1 week after service, replies within 3 days, fully briefed at least 2 weeks before trial. Criminal cases make similar joint submissions 30 days before trial. A final pretrial conference is held about 2 weeks before trial; trial counsel must attend and be ready to discuss settlement in civil cases.

docs.t: Judge Victor Marrero (S.D.N.Y.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Victor Marrero, S.D.N.Y.. Trial: Trials run Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., lunch about 12:45 to 2 p.m., Courtroom 15B. Requests to bring laptops or other devices are due by letter at least 10 calendar days ahead (presumptive limit of 3 per party). Openings are limited to 15 minutes absent unusual complexity. In civil cases the defendant closes first, and the plaintiff follows without rebuttal. Bench trials: direct testimony by affidavit only with permission, and lists of affiants to be cross-examined are due 5 business days before trial. Pre-mark exhibits (“P. Ex.” numbers, “D. Ex.” letters) and give the clerk two complete sets of trial binders on day one. Only one attorney per side per witness; refer to everyone by surname; offer stipulations privately. Juries are chosen by the struck panel method (civil panels of 12, 16, or 18 for 6, 8, or 10 jurors); peremptories can be wai

Mark each “Courtesy Copy” with case name, docket number, and ECF numbers. Exhibits tabbed and indexed and bound separately from the brief; papers under 35 pages stapled, not bound. docs.t: Judge Colleen McMahon (S.D.N.Y.) — Communications (trap)

ECF filings are generally reviewed the next business day; if a filing needs faster attention, call chambers after filing. No faxes of motion papers unless directed, and nothing over 10 pages without authorization.

docs.x: Judge Colleen McMahon, S.D.N.Y.. Motion practice (trap): No return dates: opposition is due 14 days after receipt of the moving papers and reply 5 days later. File papers promptly after service; do not hold them until briefing is complete. docs.t: Judge Colleen McMahon (S.D.N.Y.) — Summary judgment and Daubert
docs.x: Judge Colleen McMahon, S.D.N.Y.. Summary judgment and Daubert: SJ motions are due no later than 30 days after the close of discovery (the 2022 case management plan form instead bars service after the pretrial order date). Filing SJ does not excuse or extend the pretrial order deadline. Submit only the deposition pages actually cited, each tabbed and indexed. Opposing 56.1 statements must reproduce each movant’s paragraph with the response beneath it; additional facts continue the numbering. A joint 56.1 statement of agreed facts is strongly encouraged. Material merely delivered to chambers but not filed is not part of the record. Daubert motions must be made by the dispositive-motion deadline, not as motions in limine.

docs.t: Judge Colleen McMahon (S.D.N.Y.) — Qualified immunity (trap)
docs.x: Judge Colleen McMahon, S.D.N.Y.. Qualified immunity (trap): A pre-discovery qualified immunity motion must accept the plaintiff’s non-conclusory facts as true and argue the law was unsettled; motions arguing the conduct was lawful are summarily denied. File a bare notice of motion (listing all grounds) at the earliest opportunity, with no brief. Defendants must depose the plaintiff within 30 days of the notice (normally the plaintiff’s only deposition), then brief within 30 days; plaintiff responds within 30 days and defendants file an omnibus reply within 14 days. No defense or third-party affidavits; only the plaintiff’s deposition is considered. Failure to follow these rules waives pre-trial judgment on qualified immunity. Otherwise plead it as a defense and move after discovery on the summary judgment schedule.

docs.t: Judge Colleen McMahon (S.D.N.Y.) — Initial conference and case types
docs.x: Judge Colleen McMahon, S.D.N.Y.. Initial conference and case types: Initial conferences are held by phone unless the parties request in person. If the parties file an agreed case management plan on the judge’s form at least 2 days before, the conference is canceled once the plan is signed (not if a fully briefed motion is pending). Discovery must normally finish within 6 months of filing; extensions are not routine, even if stipulated. Diversity cases: before the initial conference or any dispositive motion, a letter of up to 2 pages establishing citizenship (all members of LLCs, partnerships, and other unincorporated entities). Removing parties must supply courtesy copies of state-court pleadings. Related cases carry both docket numbers. Do not use the standard plan in RICO, patent, FLSA collective, ERISA, IDEA, Rule B, administrative appeal, arbitration, or PSLRA cases. RICO plaintiffs

Discovery and confidentiality (trap): At the first discovery dispute, file an ECF letter asking for a reference to the magistrate judge, then go there directly. Disputes never extend the discovery deadline, and only Judge McMahon can extend it in non-pro se cases. Notify the judge by letter when filing Rule 72 objections. The judge’s e-discovery rules apply automatically unless superseded by consent order: exchange custodians, systems, and retention information before the Rule 16 conference; designate an e-discovery liaison by the first answer date; file retention compliance statements within 7 days of identifying custodians; default production as image files. The judge will sign a confidentiality stipulation only with the posted addendum: the record is presumed public, and decisions referring to confidential material are held 10 days for the parties to j

docs.t: Judge Colleen McMahon (S.D.N.Y.) — Extensions and appearances
docs.x: Judge Colleen McMahon, S.D.N.Y.. Extensions and appearances: Adjournment requests at least 48 hours before the appearance; extension requests at least 2 days before the deadline, by ECF letter motion stating the original date, prior requests and outcomes, adversary’s position, and effect on other dates (attach a revised scheduling order). Late requests are not entertained absent a true emergency. Requests to appear by phone must be made on ECF at least 2 days (2 business days under the 2016 procedures) before, stating the reason; never granted for trials or evidentiary hearings. The 2016 procedures route approved appearances through CourtCall by noon the day before.

docs.t: Judge Colleen McMahon (S.D.N.Y.) — Pretrial and in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge Colleen McMahon, S.D.N.Y.. Pretrial and in limine (trap): The joint pretrial order (Annex A form) with two courtesy copies is due on the scheduled date, ordinarily 30 days after discovery ends; lateness may bring dismissal or default. File the same day requests to charge, voir dire, and a verdict form (jury) or elements-and-facts statements (non-jury), each with one hard copy. In limine motions may not be filed with the pretrial order: file within 5 days after notice of the final pretrial conference, with responses 5 days later and no replies. One notice of motion per ruling, with a brief of no more than 5 pages and a supporting affidavit; no omnibus motions. Trial counsel must attend the FPTC (only they may try the case) and be ready for trial on 24 hours’ phone notice. Provide pre-marked exhibits (PX/DX), one set for the adversary and two for the court, at least 5 days before the

docs.t: Judge Colleen McMahon (S.D.N.Y.) — Trial and bench trials
docs.x: Judge Colleen McMahon, S.D.N.Y.. Trial and bench trials: Trials run Monday to Thursday, 9:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.; a party out of witnesses must rest. Struck-panel jury selection with the court questioning; in most civil cases the parties exercise 4 peremptory challenges in alternating rounds and the 8 lowest-numbered remaining jurors serve. Civil parties must arrange their own interpreters and technology; devices require a court order sought by ECF letter. Bench trials: proposed findings and conclusions, trial memoranda (up to 25 pages), and narrative direct-testimony statements for witnesses under a party’s control, due 20 days before the FPTC (the rules elsewhere say statements 10 days before). Witnesses adopt their statements under oath, then face cross. Evidentiary hearings follow the same procedure, with papers 10 days and exhibits 5 days before.

docs.t: Judge Colleen McMahon (S.D.N.Y.) — Criminal sentencing
docs.x: Judge Colleen McMahon, S.D.N.Y.. Criminal sentencing: Defense sentencing submissions are served 2 weeks and the government’s 1 week before sentencing, with one courtesy copy. Letters are filed together under one SENTENCING MEMORANDUM; redactions beyond the eleven Privacy Policy categories require an application served with the submission.

docs.t: Judge Loretta Preska (S.D.N.Y.) — Pre-motion conferences (trap)
docs.x: Judge Loretta Preska, S.D.N.Y.. Pre-motion conferences (trap): A pre-motion conference is required before any non-discovery motion. The movant’s letter may not exceed 1,050 words; the non-movant responds within 3 business days in up to 1,050 words; the movant may reply within 1 business day in up to 700 words. The movant must remind the non-movant of its duty to respond. Exceptions: incarcerated pro se litigants, TROs, injunctions, motions to dismiss in lieu of answer, remand, reargument, FRAP 4(a)(4)(A) motions, attorneys’ fees, sentence reductions, objections to magistrate judge rulings, petitions to compel arbitration or confirm or modify awards, orders to show cause, pro hac vice, and PSLRA lead-counsel motions. Discovery motions follow Local Civil Rule 37.2. Handwritten or typewritten letters from unrepresented parties are limited to 3 pages (reply 2).

docs.t: Judge Loretta Preska (S.D.N.Y.) — Briefs and motion practice (trap)
docs.x: Judge Loretta Preska, S.D.N.Y.. Briefs and motion practice (trap): Memoranda are limited to 7,000 words and replies to 3,500 words, in at least 12-point type for text and footnotes. Memoranda of 3,500 words or more need a table of contents and table of authorities. Handwritten or typewritten pro se briefs: 20 pages, replies 10. File motion papers promptly after service. Request oral argument by letter when filing your papers; the court decides whether to hear it. The court encourages junior lawyers to argue and may allow more than one lawyer per side for that purpose; say so in the argument request. Default judgments follow Local Civil Rules 55.1 and 55.2, and the movant must also provide a proposed Order to Show Cause.

docs.x: Judge Loretta Preska, S.D.N.Y.. Letters and contacting chambers (trap): Letters go on ECF, in at least 14-point type (text and footnotes); do not also send a paper copy of an ECF letter. Letters filed under seal or seeking sealing, letters with sensitive or confidential information, and pro se letters go to chambers by mail, with copies to all counsel. (The rules also mention fax for these, but say faxes are not permitted.) For docketing, scheduling, and calendar matters, email the courtroom deputy at PreskaNYSDChambers@nysd.uscourts.gov. For questions the rules don’t answer or urgent matters, email that inbox to request the court’s telephone contact information. Do not copy the court on correspondence between counsel.

docs.t: Judge Loretta Preska (S.D.N.Y.) — Adjournments and extensions
docs.x: Judge Loretta Preska, S.D.N.Y.. Adjournments and extensions: Absent an emergency, request adjournments or extensions at least 48 hours before the deadline. State the original date, the number of prior requests, whether they were granted or denied, and whether the adversary consents (and if not, why). If other dates are affected, attach a proposed Revised Scheduling Order reflecting only business days.

docs.t: Judge Loretta Preska (S.D.N.Y.) — Sealing: paper filing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Loretta Preska, S.D.N.Y.. Sealing: paper filing (trap): The motion or letter-motion to seal is filed publicly on ECF, with reasons and without the confidential material, but the proposed sealed documents are filed in the traditional manner, on paper. For redactions, contemporaneously file the redacted version publicly on ECF. Contemporaneously hand deliver or email to PreskaNYSDChambers@nysd.uscourts.gov the proposed sealed or redacted document, a copy of the motion, and supporting papers.
